title: The great supper (Luke 14:15–24)
hook: the invited make excuses, and the poor, lame and blind are brought in

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seating chart, and the last place at the table. Your line was invite the ones who can't repay.

You've planned a party. Everyone said yes, and you've cooked all day. Then, an hour before, the texts start. So sorry, something came up. Rain check? Then another. Then another. You're standing in a kitchen full of food with an empty room. At the same dinner as yesterday, a guest says something pious: blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God. And Jesus answers with a story about exactly that kitchen.
screen: `THE TEXTS START AN HOUR BEFORE.` → `A KITCHEN FULL OF FOOD.` → `AN EMPTY ROOM.`

segments.voice: A man makes a great supper and invites many. When it's ready, his servant goes out: come, all is ready. And they all, Luke says, begin to make excuse. I've bought a farm and I need to go see it. I've bought five yoke of oxen, and I'm going to try them out. I've married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. Some readers notice how thin these sound: who buys a farm before seeing it, or oxen before trying them? The host is angry, but he doesn't cancel. He sends the servant into the streets and lanes of the city: bring in the poor, the maimed, the blind and the lame, exactly yesterday's guests. The servant comes back: done, and there's still room. So the master says: "Go out into the highways and hedges; and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled." That line has a hard history. Centuries later, compel was read as permission to force people into the faith. Saint Augustine, in a bitter fight with the Donatists in North Africa, used this verse to defend pressure from the state. The Church today reads it differently: the Second Vatican Council taught that no one may be forced to embrace the faith against their will. Read inside the story, compel sounds like the host's urgency, not violence: the servant goes out to people on the roadsides who would hardly expect an invitation, and has to insist. And at Mass, just before Communion, the priest holds up the host and says that those called to the supper of the Lamb are blessed, words drawn from the Book of Revelation.
screen: `COME, ALL IS READY.` · `A FARM, FIVE OXEN, A WIFE.` · `BRING IN THE POOR AND THE LAME.` · `URGENCY, NOT FORCE.` · then, large: `THAT MY HOUSE MAY BE FILLED.`

segments.voice: Think of an invitation you've been dodging: a friend's dinner, a parish event, a call from your mother. Notice the excuse you've been using, and ask whether it's a farm you have to see, or something real. If you pray, thank God for the invitations in your life.
Compel. The host's command to fill his house with the poor and the people on the roads, after the invited guests skipped his feast with thin excuses. Today's word.
Your line: compel them to come in. That's week sixty-seven: bigger barns, the lilies, fig tree, infirmity, the hen, last place, and the great supper. Day four hundred sixty-nine, done.

howItsDone: At every Mass, just before Communion, the priest invites the people with words drawn from the Book of Revelation about those called to the supper of the Lamb; some Catholic readers hear the great supper in that invitation.

fork.setup: you've cooked a great supper. every invited guest just sent an excuse. what do you do?
options: cancel and throw the food away.
send for the poor, the lame and the blind.
fork.reveal: he fills the house with people who'd never expect an invitation, and when there's still room, sends to the highways too.

trapdoor: what you thought: compel them to come in means force people into church.
what it means: in the story, compel is the host's urgency: people on the roads won't believe they're invited, so the servant insists.
what a scholar hears: Augustine cited this verse (Letter 93, Letter 185) against the Donatists; Vatican II's Dignitatis Humanae teaches no one may be coerced into faith.
recall: the jar of ointment poured on his feet

chat.says: Doesn't "compel them to come in" mean forcing people to join a church?
options: No: the Church teaches no one may be forced to believe; it's the host's urgency.
Yes, and the Church still reads it that way today, as permission to force.
No, it means only the poor will ever be let into God's kingdom.
